'''Helen Jane Wilson''',<ref name="uclhome">{{cite web|url=http://www.ucl.ac.uk/~ucahhwi/ |title=Helen Wilson's UCL home page |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170116174729/http://www.ucl.ac.uk/~ucahhwi/ |archive-date=16 January 2017 }}</ref> (born 1973), is a British mathematician and was the Head of Mathematics at [[University College London]] (UCL).

Her research focuses on the theoretical and numerical modelling of the flow of non-Newtonian fluids such as polymeric materials and particle suspensions.

== Early life and education ==
Wilson was born in [[Warrington]]. Her father, Leslie Knight Wilson was a chartered accountant; her mother, Brenda (née Naylor) a French teacher. She attended Broomfields Junior School and Bridgewater High School.
Wilson studied at [[Clare College, Cambridge|Clare College]], [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]], completing a BA, [[Part III of the Mathematical Tripos|Certificate of Advanced Study in Mathematics]] (later converted to an MMath) and PhD in mathematics. Her PhD thesis, titled "Shear Flow Instabilities in Viscoelastic Fluids", was supervised by John Rallison. On graduation she moved to the University of Colorado at Boulder, where she began research on suspension mechanics with Rob Davis in the Chemical Engineering department.

== Mathematical work ==
In 2000 Wilson returned to the UK to take up a lectureship in Applied Mathematics at the University of Leeds.
In 2004 she moved to UCL,<ref name="uclhome"/> where she is Professor of Applied Mathematics and from 2018 to 2023 Head of department. Wilson is the first woman to hold the position of Head of Mathematics at UCL.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ucl.ac.uk/mathematical-physical-sciences/spotlight-professor-helen-wilson|title=Spotlight on Professor Helen Wilson|last=UCL|date=2019-02-01|website=UCL Mathematical & Physical Sciences|language=en|access-date=2019-02-04}}</ref><ref> {{Cite web|url=https://www.ucl.ac.uk/mathematical-physical-sciences/case-studies/2023/dec/professor-christian-boehmer|title=Professor Christian Gerhard Boehmer is the new Head of Department of Mathematics.|last=UCL|date=2023-12-01|website=UCL Mathematical & Physical Sciences|language=en|access-date=2026-06-19}}</ref>

===Research in fluid mechanics===

Wilson's PhD thesis and early papers focused on instabilities in [[viscoelastic]] fluids. She predicted a new instability in channel flow of a shear-thinning fluid<ref name="shearthininst">{{cite journal|last1=Wilson|first1=Helen J|last2=Rallison|first2=John M|title=Instability of channel flow of a shear-thinning White-Metzner fluid|journal=Journal of Non-Newtonian Fluid Mechanics|year=1999|volume=87|pages=75–96|doi=10.1016/S0377-0257(99)00012-9|url=http://www.ucl.ac.uk/~ucahhwi/publist/papers/1999-WR-a.pdf|citeseerx=10.1.1.582.7978}}</ref> which was later discovered experimentally by another group<ref name="bodiguelexperiments">{{cite journal|last1=Bodiguel|first1=Hugues|last2=Beaumont|first2=Julien|last3=Machado|first3=Anais|last4=Martinie|first4=Laetitia|last5=Kellay|first5=Hamid|last6=Colin|first6=Annie|title=Flow Enhancement due to Elastic Turbulence in Channel Flows of Shear Thinning Fluids|journal=Physical Review Letters|year=2015|volume=114|issue=2|article-number=028302|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.114.028302|pmid=25635567|bibcode=2015PhRvL.114b8302B|url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01105020/file/BodiguesPRL2015_114-028302.pdf}}</ref> and on which she still works. She has also worked on instabilities in shear-banding flows and in more complex geometries.

Her other major research interest, besides viscoelasticity, is suspension mechanics, and in particular the effect of particle contacts on fluid rheology. Her most recent projects <ref name="academichomepage">{{cite web|url=http://www.ucl.ac.uk/~ucahhwi/ |title=Prof Helen J Wilson: Homepage |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170116174729/http://www.ucl.ac.uk/~ucahhwi/ |archive-date=16 January 2017 }}</ref> draw these two fields together, investigating the interaction of solid particles with their complex material environment in fields ranging from healthcare to engineering.

Her academic publications are listed on the UCL site.<ref name="pubs">{{cite web|url=https://iris.ucl.ac.uk/iris/browse/profile?upi=HWILS67 |title=Helen Wilson's publications |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170116174809/https://iris.ucl.ac.uk/iris/browse/profile?upi=HWILS67 |archive-date=16 January 2017 }}</ref>

One of her best-known publications is the paper "The fluid dynamics of the chocolate fountain",<ref name="choc">{{cite journal|last1=Townsend|first1=Adam K|last2=Wilson|first2=Helen J.|title=The fluid dynamics of the chocolate fountain|journal=European Journal of Physics|year=2015|volume=37|issue=1|article-number=015803|doi=10.1088/0143-0807/37/1/015803|doi-access=free}}</ref> co-authored with Adam Townsend.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://adamtownsend.com |title=Adam Townsend's web site |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161026083632/http://adamtownsend.com/ |archive-date=26 October 2016 }}</ref> Unusually for a mathematical paper, this was covered in the Washington Post.<ref>{{cite news| url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/speaking-of-science/wp/2015/11/24/someone-finally-looked-into-the-physics-of-chocolate-fountains/?tid=ss_tw | title= Washington Post: Speaking of Science. Someone finally looked into the physics of chocolate fountains| newspaper= [[The Washington Post]]}}</ref>

===Knowledge transfer===
Wilson gave the 2019 Joint [[London Mathematical Society]] Annual Lecture on "Toothpaste, custard and chocolate: mathematics gets messy".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gresham.ac.uk/lectures-and-events/mathematics-gets-messy|title=Toothpaste, Custard and Chocolate: Mathematics Gets Messy|website=www.gresham.ac.uk|access-date=2019-10-09}}</ref>

Problem plastics & how mathematics can help,<ref>{{cite web|last1=Wilson|first1=Helen|title=Problem plastics -and how mathematics can help|url=http://www.ucl.ac.uk/~ucahhwi/uclscience.html|publisher=UCL|access-date=5 January 2017}}</ref> published in UCL Science and presented at Mathematics Works (Oct 2007).

Public lecture: From gases to gloops: Instabilities in fluids in the UCL Lunch Hour Lecture series on 23 February 2016.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Wilson|first1=Helen|title=From gases to gloops: instabilities in fluids|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eT2H91huOA8|publisher=UCL Lunch hour lectures|access-date=5 January 2017}}</ref>

===Non-technical articles===

Case study for the Royal Society<ref>{{cite web|last1=Wilson|first1=Helen|title=Return to work after maternity leave: departmental actions that eased the transition and therefore made retention so much more likely|url=https://royalsociety.org/~/media/policy/projects/leading-the-way/case-studies/helen-wilson-case-study.pdf?la=en-GB|publisher=Royal Society|access-date=5 January 2017}}</ref> on how a supportive employer can support a mother on her return to work.

Blog post<ref>{{cite web|last1=Wilson|first1=Helen|title=The Fields Medal: a stepping stone for women in mathematics|url=http://blogs.ucl.ac.uk/science/2014/08/14/the-fields-medal-a-stepping-stone-for-women-in-mathematics/|publisher=UCL|access-date=5 January 2017}}</ref> and BBC World TV news interview<ref>{{cite web|last1=BBC TV World News|title=Interview with Helen Wilson|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s5dpyqsgN6I|via=YouTube|access-date=5 January 2017}}</ref> commenting on the award of the Fields Medal to a female mathematician for the first time.

The [[D'Hondt method]] Explained:<ref>{{cite web|last1=Wilson|first1=Helen|title=The D'Hondt Method Explained|url=http://www.ucl.ac.uk/~ucahhwi/dhondt.pdf|publisher=UCL}}</ref> brief explanation of an easier way to understand the allocation of seats at the European elections

===Books===
Practical Analytical Methods for PDEs in volume 1 of the LTCC Advanced Mathematics series, World Scientific, 2015.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Helen Wilson|author-link1=Practical Analytical Methods for PDEs|editor1-last=Bullett|editor1-first=S.R.|editor2-last=Fearn|editor2-first=Tom|editor3-last=Smith|editor3-first=Frank|title=Advanced Techniques in Applied Mathematics|date=2015|chapter=Practical Analytical Methods for PDEs}}</ref>

In 2016, Wilson co-authored with Dame [[Celia Hoyles]] a chapter of the book "Mathematics: How It Shaped Our World"<ref>{{cite book|editor1-last=Rooney|editor1-first=David|title=Mathematics: How it Shaped Our World|date=22 December 2016|publisher=Scala Arts & Heritage Publishers Ltd|isbn=978-1-78551-039-7|url=https://www.sciencemuseumshop.co.uk/home/books_prints_and_stationery/mathematics-how-it-shaped-our-world-book.htm}}</ref>

== Recognition ==
Wilson was president (for the 2015–2017 term) of the [[British Society of Rheology]]<ref>[http://www.bsr.org.uk/council.asp Council] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170112170821/http://www.bsr.org.uk/council.asp |date=12 January 2017 }}, British Society of Rheology'. Retrieved 4 January 2017.</ref>
the first woman to hold this position.

In 2014 she was a member of the subject panel for Mathematics on ALCAB (the A Level Content Advisory Board), advising on the reforms to A Level Mathematics for first teaching in September 2016.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://alcab.org.uk/our-people/subject-panels/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171006045210/http://alcab.org.uk/our-people/subject-panels/|archive-date=6 October 2017|title=The A-Level Content Advisory Board|access-date=4 January 2017|url-status=live}}</ref>

She was a Council Member and is now the vice-president (Learned Societies) of the [[Institute of Mathematics and its Applications]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ima.org.uk/about_us/governance/council.cfm.html|title = Council Archives| date=24 May 2023 }}</ref>
